title: About
text:
Jessica De Rongé holds a Master’s degree in Political Science from UCLouvain, obtained in 2021, and a Master’s degree in Statistics from UCLouvain, obtained in 2024. Since October 2024, she has been a PhD student at the Centre for European Studies and Comparative Politics (CEE). As part of her PhD research, she investigates citizen trust in various mechanisms of citizen participation, such as mini-publics. Previously, she worked on youth participation in the Youth for Climate movement and on the cultural equivalence of the concept of political efficacy.
Paul Servais holds a degree in Physical Engineering from the Université Libre de Bruxelles (2023) and a Master’s in Governance of Ecological Transitions from the École Urbaine de Sciences Po Paris (2025). In 2025, he worked as a research assistant for Carlo Colombo on the ‘GUD EU Law’ project. He specializes in political science, with a focus on comparative politics. Paul Servais is preparing a PhD in comparative political science, examining the direct and indirect effects of climate change on political behavior in Western Europe.

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
The canonical form of a research enigma, or research puzzle, lays in this simple relationship : a dependent variable X, remains puzzling despite knowing a series of relationships, X that affect this variable. The researcher’s task generally comes with identifying an other variable, Z - or series of variables -, which might explain and cause X, despite knowing Y. That is generally how a research project can be formulated : why Y despite X ? Because Z.
The typical task of a research problem is therefore to link dependent variables with explanatory variables, Z, and to distinguish them from other types of variables, X, which do typically originate from previous research or the researcher’s intuition, and which might also affect the variable Y. Of course, isolating such causation relationships is anything but trivial, and the whole point of this semester’s class will be to convince you that correlation and causation have nothing in common.
The most used model in quantitative social science to establish such causation relationships is called the linear regression model: it is the workhorse of quantitative analysis in social science. This model generally assumes that X and Y evolve together in a linear way - that is, any increase in X, noted \(\Delta X\), has an impact \(\beta \Delta X\) on \(Y\), where \(\beta\) is constant. The objective of this session is therefore to :

remind you some basics in R
remind you some basics in descriptive statistics
remind you what simple regressions and multiple regressions

All these notions will be crucial for the rest of the semester.

title: Quantitative methods II
text:
This website supports the teaching of the class of quantitative methods II, taught in the School of Research of Sciences Po. The tutorials are supporting the theoretical class given by Jan Rovny and Brenda Van Coppennolle, and aims to remind students notions about R, OLS regressions, as well as to introduce them to causal inference methods used in social science, all based on practical coding exercices on R. This class is built on numerous sources that have contributed to inspire our theory and exercices.
From current or former instructors of SciencesPo, an introduction to R coding is available on Malo Jan’s website (RStudio introduction course). Different coding examples are also provided by Jan Rovny, on his website. This class has also been taught last year by Luis Sattelmayer, whose site provides detailed information, exercices appendices, from which this website is often directly or indirectly inspired. Moreover, there exists a wealth of ressources online, which have also guided the making of this class. To cite only but a few of them :

Cunningham, Scott. Causal Inference: The Mixtape. (2021). Available at: https://mixtape.scunning.com/.

Huntington-Klein. The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality. (2021). https://theeffectbook.net/
https://scpoecon.github.io/ScPoEconometrics/R-intro.html

Though this class is considered “advanced”, it is also thought of and conceived as a way to remind important notions in statistics, as well as basics of coding, already seen in the class of quantitative methods I. So rest reassured that, as much as we can, we will (1) remind previous notions of coding and statistics, (2) advance in a rhythm that is suitable for everyone.
The teaching assistants for this class are :

Jessica de Rongé, who is reachable at jessica.deronge@sciencespo.fr
Paul Servais, who can be contacted at paul.servais@sciencespo.fr

title: Quantitative methods II
text:
Homeworks
In order to assess your progress throughout the semester, two homeworks - each worth 15% of the final grade -, will be organised at the end of week 2, and at the end of week 4. You will receive the guidelines for these homeworks at that moment, and you will have two weeks (hence, until the next session) to upload your solutions to these problems on Moodle. These homeworks will be conceived to only check your advancement in the class, and not to overload you with burdensome work. Our goal is absolutely not to overload you with work, but mainly to control for your engagement with the course material. Don’t be worried if you don’t manage to fully complete the exercices or if your code is imperfect, we understand and know that getting into coding can be hard and that there is a quite high entry cost to this kind of course content - our main ambition for you is that you try and get your hands in the mud - otherwise coding is impossible to learn.

Base R
R is a language that comes with a basic infrastructure, which is called Base R, and is able to perform a wide array of basic tasks. This basic infrastructure is the basic tools that you get when you download R. In order to facilitate everyone’s life, very nice and smart people have built additional coding tools, which we only have to install, and that allow us to perform complex tasks in an extremely fast and elegant manner.

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
Interpretation of regression results
Here, you see that we have many information. The first thing we want to identify is the structure of the table. In the left column, we have our independent variable—our predictor. On the right-hand side, we have the corresponding coefficients, some of which have stars. In parentheses and underneath each coefficient, we find the standard errors. Smaller standard errors suggest more precise estimates.
The stars tell us something about statistical significance. If a variable has a p-value below a certain threshold, it will be marked with one or more stars. A single star * denotes significance at the 5% level (p < 0.05), two stars ** indicate significance at the 1% level (p < 0.01), and three stars *** show significance at the 0.1% level (p < 0.001). This means that a specific variable has a statistically significant relationship with the dependent variable and contributes to explaining its variance. However, the absence of statistical significance does not necessarily mean that the variable has no effect—it may suggest that there is insufficient evidence to detect a meaningful relationship given the data.
The coefficients tell us about the direction and strength of the association between a statistically significant predictor and our dependent variable. A positive coefficient indicates that an increase in the independent variable is associated with an increase in the dependent variable, while a negative coefficient suggests that an increase in the independent variable corresponds to a decrease in the dependent variable. Since this is an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, we can interpret the coefficients directly. However, because the independent variable is logged, the interpretation must be made in proportional (percentage) terms rather than in raw units.
Let’s interpret the above regression table. Always bear in mind what a change of values would correspond to on the measurement scale of your dependent variable. In our case, higher values of the dependent variable correspond to a higher share of votes for far-right parties.
Household income (logged) is negatively and highly significantly associated with the share of far-right votes. The coefficient is −0.186 and is statistically significant at the 0.1% level. This means that, in intermediate urban areas, an increase in average household income is associated with a decrease in far-right electoral support. More precisely, a 1% increase in average household income is associated with approximately a 0.19-point decrease in the share of far-right votes. This suggests that wealthier municipalities tend to vote less for far-right parties.
The intercept represents the expected level of far-right vote share when the logged income variable equals zero. While this value (2.31) is not substantively meaningful on its own, it is necessary for correctly estimating the relationship between income and far-right voting.
Bear in mind that this model is a very simple one. It includes only one independent variable and is therefore likely to omit many important predictors of far-right voting, such as education levels, unemployment, age structure, immigration levels, or political history. As a result, the model may suffer from omitted variable bias, meaning that the estimated effect of income may be capturing the influence of other unobserved factors correlated with income. While the negative association is strong and statistically significant, it should not be interpreted as a causal effect.
There is also some additional information in the table that tells us more about the model’s fit and overall performance:

R²: The R-squared value is 0.263, meaning that approximately 26.3% of the variation in far-right vote share across intermediate urban areas is explained by average household income alone. This is relatively high for a single-variable model, suggesting that income is an important correlate of far-right voting.
Adjusted R²: The adjusted R-squared (0.2632) is almost identical to the R-squared value, which is expected given that the model includes only one predictor. This indicates that the explanatory power of the model is not artificially inflated by unnecessary variables.
Residual Standard Error: The residual standard error is 0.084, which measures the average distance between the model’s predicted values and the observed far-right vote shares. Lower values indicate better predictive accuracy; here, the error suggests a moderate level of unexplained variation remains.
F-statistic: The F-statistic is very large (1248) and highly statistically significant, indicating that the model performs far better than a model with no predictors at all. In other words, income significantly improves our ability to explain variation in far-right electoral support.

Overall, this regression suggests a strong and statistically significant negative relationship between household income and far-right voting in intermediate urban areas, while also highlighting the limits of inference from a highly simplified model.

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
Interactions
You may now wonder how heterogeneous your results are, depending on one another. Indeed, perhaps the effect of income on the far-right vote is conditional on another variable, that is for instance the level of education ; and vice-versa. In other words, the results might be heterogeneous : a rich commune with less educated people can potentially vote differently than a rich commune with many higher educated persons. This is what is meant by checking for interactions between independent variables. For instance, in the case of a regression model with three variables, instead of checking :
\[\begin{equation}
Y_i = \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \beta_3 X_{3i},
\end{equation}\]
you try : \[\begin{equation}
Y_i = \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \beta_3 X_{3i} + \beta_4 X_{1i}*X_{3i}
\end{equation}\]
Which means that any increase \(\Delta X_{1i}\) in the variable \(X_{1i}\) no longer has an impact \(\beta_1 \Delta X_{1i}\) on \(Y_i\), but an impact \(\Delta X_{1i} (\beta_1 + \beta_3X_{3i})\), which therefore still depends on the variable \(X_{3i}\). Coming back to our example, we want to assess how income and education in a commune evolve and influence far-right voting. You only need to specify * in your regression to obtain the interaction :

model3 <- lm(data = elections2024 %>% filter(dens == "Urbain intermédiaire") %>% 
               mutate(petr = etranger/pop, psup = sup/pop, pnodip = nodip/pop, log_revmoyfoy = log(revmoyfoy)),
             far_right_relvotes ~ log_revmoyfoy +petr+ pagri+pouvr+ pcadr+age+log(prixbien)+pempl+ppint+pindp+psup+pnodip + log_revmoyfoy*psup)

library(ggeffects)

ggpredict(model3, terms = c("log_revmoyfoy", "psup")) |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(
    group = factor(
      group,
      levels = c("0.14", "0.23", "0.32"),
      labels = c(
        "Low share of higher education (14%)",
        "Medium share of higher education (23%)",
        "High share of higher education (32%)"
      )
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x, predicted, color = group, fill = group)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    color = "Share with higher education",
    fill  = "Share with higher education"
  )








And you see that your predicted values change with the level of education : in the more educated cases, the line becomes less steep. Here, only three values of education are plotted by the program to give an idea of the interaction in three scenarios (commune with low/medium/high proportion of educated people), but this shows that the more educated people there are in a commune, the less the impact of income on the RN vote will be important in that commune.

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
The ecological fallacy
It is important to note that, since your observations are at the commune level, your conclusions can only be drawn at the commune level. As such, even if you observe a strong correlation between RN vote share and the presence of blue-collar workers at the commune level, this does not allow you to conclude that blue-collar workers are more likely to vote for the radical right. This would be an example of the ecological fallacy, which consists of deriving individual-level behavior from aggregate-level data.
In fact, the presence of blue-collar workers in these communes may be correlated with other factors that also affect the RN vote : like living on the country-side, where other categories of the population might vote RN - and therefore lead to a strong correlation between working class voting behaviour and RN voting. It is only thanks to other studies using individual-level data that we know that the RN is the preferred party among workers (after abstention).

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
Multicollinearity
It’s essential to evaluate the correlation between predictors in regression analysis, as highly correlated predictors can introduce multicollinearity. This occurs when predictors capture overlapping information, which can distort the reliability of the model’s estimates.
A useful tool for diagnosing multicollinearity is the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), which measures how much the variance of a regression coefficient increases due to correlation among predictors. A VIF value above 10 generally signals problematic multicollinearity. Another helpful metric is tolerance (calculated as 1/VIF), which indicates the proportion of a predictor’s variance not explained by other predictors. Tolerance values near 1 suggest low collinearity. If multicollinearity is detected, techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) can help address the issue.
In R, you can assess multicollinearity using the check_collinearity() function from the performance package (or the car::vif function). These functions compute VIF, provide confidence intervals, and calculate tolerance for each predictor.

map(list(model1, model2), check_collinearity)

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
Heteroskedasticity
Heteroskedasticity occurs in regression analysis when the spread of the residuals (or errors) varies depending on the values of the independent variables. This contradicts the classical linear regression assumption of homoskedasticity, which requires that the residuals have a constant variance.
When heteroskedasticity is present, it can undermine the accuracy of statistical conclusions. The standard errors of the estimated coefficients may become unreliable, resulting in misleading p-values and confidence intervals. To detect heteroskedasticity, you can use diagnostic tools like plotting residuals against predicted values. Statistical tests, such as the Breusch-Pagan test, can also formally evaluate whether the residuals’ variance remains constant. If heteroskedasticity is confirmed, you may need to adjust the model, apply data transformations, or use robust standard errors to mitigate its impact.

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS
text:
Assumptions
For this relation to hold, the following hypotheses must be true :

\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i) = 0\). That basically means that the expectation of the error should be (there is no systematic error in your estimation).
\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i^2) = \sigma^2\). That means that the variance of the error is constant accross all values. This condition is called ‘homoskedasticity’. The case where \(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i^2) \ne \sigma^2\) is called heteroskedasticity.
\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i \epsilon_j)= 0\) or \(\mathbb{C}ov(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j) = 0\), which is called the linear independence of the errors assumption.
\(X_{ij}\) is non random \(\forall  i = 1,...,n ; j = 1, ..., k\) (X is not a random variable, contrary to the error and the dependent variable).
\(\text{rank}((X_{ij})) = k\). This is the mathematical way to say that the different independent variables are indeed independent from one another. That means that there is no way to obtain any \(X_j\) using sums and combinations of all the other \(X_k\) (where \(k \ne j\)). You will understand that later, in the last section of this class.

title: Session 1 — R reminder and OLS

Linear regression in R
Luckily for us, the linear estimator is present in base R, it’s called lm and we can use it straight for estimating regression coefficients : we just need to give our data-set and the relationship between our dependent and independent variable, and the machine does the rest for us ! We can also complete our initial graph with the geom_smooth function, that will draw this line that is the best line fitting the data, for us.

title: Quantitative methods 2
text:
Simple linear regression model

Your relation between your two variables : \[\begin{equation}
Y_i = f(X_i) + \epsilon_i
\end{equation}\]
A linear function of \(X\) is simply a function that associates a constant value \(\beta\) such that each increase \(\Delta X\) produces a \(\beta \Delta X\) on Y, so that \(\Delta Y = \beta \Delta X\). In other words, \(f(X, \epsilon) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X+\epsilon\). \[\begin{equation}
Y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i
\end{equation}\]

title: Quantitative methods 2
text:
Assumptions

The following assumptions must hold :


\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i|X_i) = \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) =  0\).
\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i^2) = \sigma^2\). Homoskedasticity.
\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i \epsilon_j)= 0\) or \(\mathbb{C}ov(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j) = 0\)
\(X_{ij}\) is non random \(\forall  i = 1,...,n ; j = 1, ..., k\)
\(\text{rank}((X_{ij})) = k\).

We want \(\beta\) (or \(f\)) that minimises the error \(\epsilon\): \[\begin{equation}

\end{equation}\]
This will give us the line that best fits the data

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
In the previous session and in our exercises, we discussed cases where our dependent variables were continuous. These included the vote share for the far-right in French communes, the median income in those communes, and party positions from the Chapel Hill survey (scaled and averaged from 1 to 10).
However, at the end of the class, we also observed that one of our results exhibited heteroskedasticity, and that plotting the residuals against the fitted values revealed some unusual shapes in the plot. This issue arises because our dependent variable, the share of votes in a commune, is bounded between 0 and 1. By default, a linear regression model does not account for these bounds, which can lead to inconsistent results (e.g., extending the regression line beyond 1, which is impossible for a share of votes), and heteroskedasticity. In situations where the dependent variable is binary, as is often the case in political science (e.g., whether someone voted or not), applying a linear regression model would violate several assumptions of the model. This is why we use logistic regression.
In practice, many dependent variables in political science are binary. A typical example is when we want to determine whether an individual voted for a particular party, or whether they voted at all. Using linear regression to analyze such variables would yield absurd results and would violate multiple assumptions underlying the model.
For this reason, we use other types of regressions to perform such analyses. The one we will explore today is particularly suited for binary outcomes (TRUE/FALSE or 1/0 outcomes). This is called logistic regression. You should have seen the theory behind these regressions with Prof. Rovny, but if you need a reminder, please go the last sections of this page.
The objectives of this session are :

Cleaning data: dropping rows, columns, creating and mutating variables
Building a generalized linear model (glm()); special focus on logit
Extracting and interpreting the coefficients
Visualization of results

A linear function of \(X\) is simply a function that associates a constant value \(\beta\) such that each increase \(\Delta X\) produces a \(\beta \Delta X\) on Y, so that \(\Delta Y = \beta \Delta X\). In other words, \(f(X, \epsilon) = \beta X+\epsilon\). \[\begin{equation}
Y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i
\end{equation}\]

title: Quantitative methods 2
text:
Simple linear regression model

We want \(\beta\) (or \(f\)) that minimises the error \(\epsilon\): \[\begin{equation}
\sum_i^N \epsilon_i^2 = \sum_i^N(Y_i - \beta_1 X_i - \beta_0)^2 = S(\beta_0,  \beta_1)
\end{equation}\]
This will give us the line that best fits the data
“Ordinary Least Squares” (OLS)

text:

title: Quantitative methods 2
text:
Assumptions

The following assumptions must hold :


\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i|X_i) = \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) =  0\).
\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i^2) = \sigma^2\). Homoskedasticity.
\(\mathbb{E} (\epsilon_i \epsilon_j)= 0\) or \(\mathbb{C}ov(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j) = 0\)
\(X_{ij}\) is non random \(\forall  i = 1,...,n ; j = 1, ..., k\)
\(\text{rank}((X_{ij})) = k\).

Exercice 2
The Chapel Hill expert survey data is a survey that “provides information about the positioning of the leadership of 279 parties in 31 countries over the course of 2024 on ideology, policy, populism, democracy, European integration, and select EU policy questions. Y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \epsilon_i

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
In the previous session and in our exercises, we discussed cases where our dependent variables were continuous. These included the vote share for the far-right in French communes, the median income in those communes, and party positions from the Chapel Hill survey (scaled and averaged from 1 to 10).
However, at the end of the class, we also observed that one of our results exhibited heteroskedasticity, and that plotting the residuals against the fitted values revealed some unusual shapes in the plot. This issue arises because our dependent variable, the share of votes in a commune, is bounded between 0 and 1. By default, a linear regression model does not account for these bounds, which can lead to inconsistent results (e.g., extending the regression line beyond 1, which is impossible for a share of votes), and heteroskedasticity. In situations where the dependent variable is binary, as is often the case in political science (e.g., whether someone voted or not), applying a linear regression model would violate several assumptions of the model. This is why we use logistic regression.
In practice, many dependent variables in political science are binary. A typical example is when we want to determine whether an individual voted for a particular party, or whether they voted at all. Using linear regression to analyze such variables would yield absurd results and would violate multiple assumptions underlying the model.
For this reason, we use other types of regressions to perform such analyses. The one we will explore today is particularly suited for binary outcomes (TRUE/FALSE or 1/0 outcomes). This is called logistic regression. You should have seen the theory behind these regressions with Prof. Rovny, but if you need a reminder, please go the last sections of this page.
The objectives of this session are :

Cleaning data: dropping rows, columns, creating and mutating variables
Building a generalized linear model (glm()); special focus on logit
Extracting and interpreting the coefficients
Visualization of results

Y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \epsilon_i

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Logistic function
The logistic function is : \[\begin{equation}
p_L (x) = \frac{1}{1+ e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(x-\mu)/s}} = \frac{e^{(x-\mu)/s}}{1+e^{(x-\mu)/s}}
\end{equation}\] and it is strictly bounded between 0 and 1, which is expected for a probability.

x <- c(1:10000)
mu <- 5000
s <- 500
plot(x, exp((x-mu)/s)/(1+exp((x-mu)/s)))








You can use this logistic function in the likelihood function: \[\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}(x) = \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 1)}^n p(x)_i \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 0)}^n (1 - p(x)_i),
\end{equation}\] maximize it, and find the parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that best fit your data.
This is the logic behind maximum likelihood estimation: you assume your probability follows a certain distribution (in this case, the logistic distribution), and then estimate the parameters that maximize the likelihood of the data. This is precisely what the glm function in R does when it fits a logistic regression model — it computes the parameters that maximize the likelihood function using numerical methods.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Logit
The logit is the inverse of the logistic function. It is defined as: \[\begin{equation}
\text{logit}(p(x)) = \ln (\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,
\end{equation}\]
The logit is the inverse of the logistic function. It is defined as:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{logit}(p(x)) = \ln \left( \frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)} \right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,
\end{equation}\]
In other words, the logit is the logarithm of the odds. The odds is simply the ratio ($ $ ), and gives a real number that tells you how many times more likely (or less likely) you are to obtain the outcome. For example, if the probability of an event occurring is 20% (i.e., ($ p = 0.2 $)), the odds are: \[\begin{equation}
\text{odds} = \frac{0.2}{1 - 0.2} = 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25.
\end{equation}\] This means the event is 4 times less likely to happen than not to happen.
On the other hand, if the probability of an event occurring is 80% (i.e., ($ p = 0.8 $)), the odds are: \[\begin{equation}
\text{odds} = \frac{0.8}{1 - 0.8} = 0.8 / 0.2 = 4.
\end{equation}\] This means the event is 4 times more likely to happen than not to happen.
When considering probabilities between 0 and 1, the odds function (\(\frac{x}{1-x}\)) increases very rapidly as the denominator approaches zero. This is why the log of the odds (the logit) provides a more manageable and continuous scale. For a visual comparison, here’s a plot in R showing the relationship between the probability (\(p\)) and the odds, as well as the logit :

p <- c(1:10000)/10000
plot(p, p/(1-p))







plot(p, log(p/(1-p)))








Hence, you see that the logit associates every probability \(p\) with a continuous variable. In the special case where the probability \(p\) is a logistic function of variables \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k\), we can express this relationship as:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{logit}(p | x_1, x_2, x_3) = \ln \left( \frac{p}{1 - p} \right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3.
\end{equation}\]
This is why you can obtain the odds by simply exponentiating the logit, which essentially gives you the odds ratio. In other words:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{ODDs} = \frac{p}{1 - p} = e^{\text{logit}(p)} = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3}.
\end{equation}\]
Any variation \(\delta x_1\) in the explanatory variable \(x_1\) leads to a change in the odds:
\[\begin{equation}
\delta \text{ODDs} = e^{\beta_1 \delta x_1}.
\end{equation}\]
This means that any change in \(x_1\) results in a multiplicative change in the odds of the outcome occurring. The model allows you to compute the probability that best characterizes your process and helps to understand how each explanatory variable influences the outcome.
Now, if you decide that \(p\) is a function of other variables \(x_1, x_2, x_3\), you need a function that associates these real numbers with probabilities that range from 0 to 1. This is exactly what the logistic regression model does — it provides a way to model the relationship between the independent variables and a binary outcome, ensuring that the probabilities stay within the valid range of 0 and 1.
But now, imagine you want to understand what drives the probability. In other words, you want to know how different factors (i.e., the explanatory variables) affect the likelihood of the outcome. The logistic regression model, through maximum likelihood estimation, gives you the answer to this question by estimating the coefficients \(\beta_1, \beta_2, \dots, \beta_k\), which tell you the effect of each variable on the log-odds of the outcome.

title: Quantitative methods 2
text:
Linear regression with interactions

Interaction : \[\begin{equation}
Y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \beta_3 X_{1i} X_{2i}  + \epsilon_i
\end{equation}\]
Any variation \(\delta X_{1i}\) translates into : \[\begin{equation}
\delta Y_i = \delta X_{1i}(\beta_1 + \beta_3 X_{2i})  
\end{equation}\]
Hence a function of \(X_{2i}\) ! The impact of \(X_{1i}\) on \(Y_i\) is changed as \(X_{2i}\) varies

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Non-constant probabilities
Now imagine that your probabilities depend on other explanatory variables \(x_1, x_2, x_3\). For example, in a research study seeking to understand voter behavior, the probability of an individual voting might depend on their income, gender, or political affiliation. In this case, you would seek to estimate the relationship between these variables and the outcome of voting.
The likelihood function in this case would be:
\[\begin{equation}
L(x_1, x_2, x_3) = \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 1)}^n p(x_1, x_2, x_3)_i \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 0)}^n (1 - p(x_1, x_2, x_3))_i
\end{equation}\]
In the simpler case where only one explanatory variable \(x\) is considered, the likelihood function is:
\[\begin{equation}
L(x) = \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 1)}^n p(x)_i \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 0)}^n (1 - p(x)_i)
\end{equation}\]
which you would maximize to find the parameters that best fit the data.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
The ESS - European Social Survey
We will be working with the European Social Survey (ESS), the largest, most comprehensive, and arguably one of the most important surveys on social and political life within the European Union. The survey is conducted in biennial waves, and each participating European country that finances the survey generates its own data. For instance, the French data (which we’ll be using from the latest, 10th wave) are produced at SciencesPo, specifically at the Centre de Données Socio-Politiques (CDSP)!
The ESS is an incredibly versatile resource, perfect for those who need a broad and detailed dataset for analyzing national politics in Europe or making cross-country comparisons. Learning how to handle, manage, and clean the ESS data will equip you with the skills to work with virtually any dataset you encounter. Additionally, many of you may find the ESS waves useful for your theses or research papers. The survey offers great potential for analysis, not just cross-sectionally but also over time. So, we encourage you to give it a try!

The variables refer to individual characteristics of the respondents, which you can find in the codebook of the ESS (provided when you download the data), either here https://stessrelpubprodwe.blob.core.windows.net/data/round8/survey/ESS8_appendix_a7_e01_1.pdf, or here <>. Some variables are straightforward, with clear names like “essround” or “age,” while others are less intuitive. Occasionally, we can infer the meaning of a variable from its name, but more often than not—either because the name is confusing or the abbreviation doesn’t make much sense—we need to refer to the dataset’s documentation. For this particular version of the dataset, you’ll find the documentation in an HTML file on Moodle (session 2).
Every high-quality, reliable dataset should have some form of documentation. If it doesn’t, it’s a red flag, and I would advise caution before using it! This documentation is typically called a “codebook.” Codebooks can vary greatly in quality—some are well-organized and easy to read, while others are a challenge to navigate. In this class, you’ll encounter both types, so you’ll be prepared to work with whatever you come across.
In general, data set you will download online will come with a codebook, basically associating each variable name with its actual name. In the case of variable gndr, the codebook for instance informs you that it means gender, and that the values refer to:

While this step can be done later, it’s often a good idea to tidy up the dataset at the very beginning, so you start with a cleaner, more manageable dataset.

You see that France has 1977 observations, which means that the sample contains about 1977 French respondents. You can restrict the data set to the French values by simply calling filter(), which will basically only keep the values that satisfy a certain condition (here cntry == "FR"), and also use table to analyse categorical values with numeric values, like vote.

And that the question that was asked to the respondents was “some people don’t vote nowadays for one reason or another. Did you vote in the last [country] national election in [month/year] ?”.
Hence, you see that 590 respondents did not vote in the last election, 1025 did and 307 were not eligible to vote.
The values 7, 8, and 9 are quite common in survey datasets. They typically represent situations where respondents either didn’t want to answer, their answer was unclear, or they couldn’t remember. You’ll encounter these values in almost every survey-based dataset.
As already said, we’ll focus on voter turnout. Our goal is to understand what factors encourage people to vote and what decreases the likelihood of voting on election day. Therefore, the question for our dependent variable will be: Did the respondent vote or not? Mathematically, this question cannot be answered using linear regression with the OLS method, as the dependent variable is binary—0 represents “did not vote” and 1 represents “voted.” There are only two possible outcomes, and the variable is not continuous, which violates one of the assumptions of OLS.
However, if we use the voting turnout variable as it is right now, we won’t have a valid binary variable. It also won’t be reliable, as it includes values that are either irrelevant or will skew our estimations. In fact, logistic regression (logit) can only be applied to binary variables.
So, before we proceed, we need to transform our dependent variable. We’ll remove unwanted values and convert the 1s and 2s into 0s and 1s.
First, we need to eliminate the values we’re not interested in. While it’s possible to filter out these values directly (as shown below), I recommend against it. Instead, you should transform these values into NA. Rows with NA values will be excluded from the regression, but if you later decide to run another model with a different dependent variable, you may lose valuable observations that you’ve filtered out. Therefore, a good rule of thumb is to only filter out values if you’re certain you’ll never need them again.

ess <- ess |>
  filter(!vote %in% c(3, 7, 8, 9))

We can directly mutate the values within the variable using case_when() inside the mutate() function. While case_when() may seem a bit tricky to read at first, it’s a powerful tool. Essentially, case_when() evaluates a series of conditions and applies the corresponding transformation to each element of a vector or column in a dataset.
Within the function, you must specify at least one condition, and you can include multiple conditions if needed. If you want the conditions to be evaluated simultaneously, use the & operator between them. If you want the condition to apply when either of two conditions is true, you would use the |`` operator. After specifying the conditions, you use a tilde~`, followed by the new value that the variable should take on if the condition is met.
Here’s how it works:

case_when(
  condition1 ~ value_if_true1,
  condition2 ~ value_if_true2,
  TRUE ~ default_value
)

Let’s look at an example below. I want the values 3, 7, 8, and 9 in the vote variable to be replaced with NA, as they are irrelevant to our analysis. To do this, we use the mutate() function, and I assign a new column (which I’ll name vote, the same as the original variable). Inside the case_when() function, I specify vote %in% c(3, 7, 8, 9) ~ NA_integer_. This statement means: whenever vote contains the values 3, 7, 8, or 9, replace them with NA_integer_.
The next line, TRUE ~ vote, serves as a catch-all rule. It says, “For all other cases, keep the original values of vote.” This ensures that any value not matching the previous condition remains unchanged.
Here’s the code:

ess <- ess |> 
  mutate(
    vote = case_when(
      vote %in% c(3, 7, 8, 9) ~ NA_integer_,
      TRUE ~ vote
  ))
table(ess$vote)


    1     2 
23529  7132 


Now, we just need to transform the ones and twos into zeros and ones. This is both a matter of convention, my personal coding preference, and, of course, to give you a bit more practice with data management. Since we are focusing on people who have voted, we’ll code those who voted as 1 and those who didn’t as 0.
We’ll use case_when() again to do this. The code case_when(vote == 1 ~ 1, vote == 2 ~ 0) works as follows: whenever vote equals 1 (indicating that the person voted), we keep it as 1; whenever vote equals 2 (indicating that the person did not vote), we assign it 0.
With that, we now have our binary dependent variable, which is essential for performing a logit. The table() function will show that we’ve successfully changed the values of the variable, but the total count remains the same.
In Base R, you could achieve this in a different way, but I personally find that using the mutate() function is the most elegant approach. That said, it’s entirely up to you which method you prefer.

# only use the ifelse() function
ess$vote <- ifelse(ess$vote == 1, 1, 0)

# This will leave the value of 1 at 1 and change 2 to 0 for the column vote.
ess$vote[ess$vote == 1] <- 1
ess$vote[ess$vote == 2] <- 0

We’re very close to finishing the data management part and getting ready to work on our model. However, there are still many variables that are as “untidy” as our initial dependent variable. We need to check the codebook to see if there are specific values we can’t simply replace across the entire dataset and whether they are still irrelevant to our analysis.
For our independent variables of interest, here’s what we need to do:

Political interest (polintr): Remove values c(7:9).
Trust in politicians (trstplt): No recoding needed (unwanted values are already NA).
Trust in political parties (trstprt): Already done.
Feeling close to a party (clsprty): Convert 1/2 to 0/1 and remove values c(7:8).
Gender (gndr): Convert to 0/1 and remove “no answer” values.
Year born (yrbrn): Already done.
Years of full-time education completed (eduyrs): Already done.

We’ll tackle all these steps at once using pipes %>% (from the tidyverse) or |> (Base R), which allows us to perform everything in a neat and efficient way. I’ll also re-run the mutation for our dependent variable to demonstrate the flexibility of long pipe chains.
We start by using mutate() to adjust the independent variables we need for our model. Notice how you can separate the different manipulations with commas inside the same function, which results in clean, readable code. There are various functions for data wrangling, such as recode(), if_else(), and case_when(). For simplicity and clarity, I’ll be using case_when() here, though there’s a newer function, case_match(), that you could also use.
Now, let’s talk about NA_integer_. In R, NA signifies “not available” or missing data. But R is very particular about the type of data it’s working with. If your variable is numeric, you need to specify that missing values should be treated as numbers. By using NA_integer_, you’re telling R, “This is missing data, but if it were here, it would be a number.” This ensures consistency and avoids confusion when R processes your data. If you’re working with character strings, you’d use NA_character_. For numeric values with decimals, you’d use NA_real_ instead of NA_integer_.

ess_final <- ess |> 
  # mutating the dependent variable to get rid of any unnecessary rows
  # as we have done above
  mutate(
    vote = case_when(
      vote %in% c(3, 7, 8, 9) ~ NA_integer_,
      vote == 2 ~ 0,
      vote == 1 ~ 1, 
      TRUE ~ vote
    ),
    # Recode 'polintr' to drop values 7 to 9
    polintr = case_when(
      polintr %in% c(7:9) ~ NA_integer_,
      TRUE ~ polintr
    ),
    # Recode 'clsprty' 1/2 into 0/1 and drop 7, 8
    clsprty = case_when(
      clsprty == 1 ~ 0,
      clsprty == 2 ~ 1,
      clsprty %in% c(7, 8) ~ NA_integer_,
      TRUE ~ clsprty
    ),
    # Recode 'gndr' into 0/1 and handle other cases as NAs
    gndr = case_when(
      gndr == 1 ~ 0,
      gndr == 2 ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    # recode eduyrs
    eduyrs = case_when(
      eduyrs %in% c(1:55) ~ eduyrs,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    # this one is very advanced...
    across(c(trstplt, trstprt), ~case_when(
      .x <= 10 ~ .x, 
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ))
  )

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Running the model
Once the data preparation is done, the best part is that running a logistic regression model literally takes just one line (or two, depending on the number of independent variables). As you’ll see, it’s quite straightforward.
The glm() function, which stands for generalized linear model, is a part of Base R.
In Professor Rovny’s lecture, we discussed that for Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), you need to know or assume the distribution of your dependent variable. Based on that distribution, you choose the appropriate linear model. For a binary outcome like voting (yes/no), the distribution is binomial. So, within the glm() function, we specify the distribution family as binomial.
It’s worth mentioning that you can specify other families, such as Gaussian, Poisson, or Gamma, depending on your data. We won’t go into detail about those families here, but the glm() function is quite powerful. By setting family = binomial(link = "logit"), we specify that we’re conducting a logistic regression. If you wanted to use a different link, such as probit or cauchy, you can easily adjust it here. The default is set to logit, so in most cases, you won’t need to specify it explicitly.
If your dependent variable is incompatible with the chosen family, the function will alert you to a problem.
For the model we’re building, we’re assuming that voting behavior (whether a person voted or not) is influenced by political interest, trust in politicians, trust in political parties, and feeling close to a party, along with typical control variables like gender, age, and education.
Please note that this regression isn’t sophisticated enough to be published—it’s simply an example. My hypothesis is that factors like political interest, trust in politics and politicians, and party affiliation are key explanatory variables.
Just like with an OLS regression, we start by specifying the dependent variable (in this case, vote). Then, we separate the dependent variable from the independent variables with a ~. Next, we list the predictors, separated by a +. Finally, we specify the data object and the model family.
Here’s how you can run the model:

logit <- glm(
  vote ~ polintr + trstplt + trstprt + clsprty + gndr +
    yrbrn + eduyrs,
  data = ess_final,
  family = "binomial")

The object we created, called logit, now contains our model along with its coefficients, confidence intervals, and many other details that we’ll explore further! As you can see, the actual process of constructing the model is incredibly simple and only requires a single line of code.
Now that we’ve created the model, we can examine its components and assess how well it fits our data. The logistic regression model has produced outputs that we can use to make inferences about the relationship between our dependent and independent variables. The simplicity of the code doesn’t mean that the analysis is complete—it’s just the beginning of our exploration!

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Interpretation of logistic regression
Interpreting the results of a logistic regression can initially feel challenging because the model predicts probabilities rather than direct outcomes. This may seem abstract at first. However, once you understand how to interpret the coefficients and odds ratios, it becomes much easier to see how the independent variables relate to the binary outcome—without necessarily transforming the coefficients into more intuitive values.

The odds ratio
To properly understand the logit, we first need to clarify what it represents: it is the logarithm of the odds. The odds themselves are defined as the ratio between the probability that an event occurs, \(p\), and the probability that it does not occur, \(1-p\).
\[\begin{equation}
\text{ODDS} = \frac{p}{1-p}
\end{equation}\]
In other words, the odds tell us how much more (or less) likely the event is to happen than not to happen. For example, if an event has a probability of 0.1, its odds are:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{ODDS} = \frac{1/10}{9/10} = 1/9
\end{equation}\]
This means the event is nine times less likely to occur than not to occur.
If the probability is 0.8, then the odds are:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{ODDS} = \frac{8/10}{2/10} = 4,
\end{equation}\]
which means the event is four times more likely to happen than not to happen. Notice that when the probability equals 0.5—meaning the event is equally likely to occur or not—the odds equal 1.
Importantly, the odds are always positive and increase very rapidly as \(p \rightarrow 1\). To obtain a more symmetric and analytically convenient measure, we usually take the natural logarithm of the odds. The logit is therefore defined as:
\[\begin{equation}
\ln(\text{ODDS}) = \ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)
\end{equation}\]
Unlike the odds, the logit can take any real value, positive or negative. The differences betweens the odds ratio function, the logit, and the logistic functions are shown in the panel below.

Odds ratioLogit functionLogistic function



p <- c(1:10000)/10000 # probabilities 0.0001, 0.0002, 0.0003,... 0.9998, 0.9999
plot(p, p/(1-p)) # odds











plot(p, log(p/(1-p))) # logit











x <- c(1:10000)
mu <- 5000
s <- 500
plot(x, exp((x-mu)/s)/(1+exp((x-mu)/s))) # logistic function











Now, suppose that the probability \(p\) follows a logistic function of some variable \(x\) (for instance, \(p\) could represent the probability of voting, and \(x\) a person’s income). Then we can write:
\[\begin{equation}
p(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{- (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}
\end{equation}\]
Taking the logit of this expression yields a simple linear relationship:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{logit}(p(x)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
\end{equation}\]
This expression corresponds to the log of the odds. By exponentiating the logit, we recover the odds:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{ODDS} = e^{\text{logit}(p(x))} = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}.
\end{equation}\]
Therefore, a change \(\delta x\) in \(x\) leads to a multiplicative change of \(e^{\beta_1 \delta x}\) in the odds. This makes interpretation straightforward: depending on the sign of \(\beta_1\), the event becomes more or less likely to occur.
Hence, in our case :

# simply use exp() on the coefficients of the logit
exp(coef(logit))

(Intercept)     polintr     trstplt     trstprt     clsprty        gndr 
 11.7462918   0.5651311   1.0370047   1.0444578   0.4235567   1.1003495 
      yrbrn      eduyrs 
  1.0000242   1.0478581 

# here would be a second way of doing it
exp(logit$coefficients)

(Intercept)     polintr     trstplt     trstprt     clsprty        gndr 
 11.7462918   0.5651311   1.0370047   1.0444578   0.4235567   1.1003495 
      yrbrn      eduyrs 
  1.0000242   1.0478581 


We can—and should—also report the 95% confidence intervals (CIs). As a brief reminder, a confidence interval provides a range of values that is likely to contain the true value of a parameter—in our case, the coefficients of the predictor variables. This range is associated with a specific level of confidence. The most commonly used confidence levels (note that this is simply a statistical convention) are 95% and, less frequently, 99%.
A 95% confidence interval means that if we were to repeatedly estimate the same logistic regression model using many different samples drawn from the same population, the true parameter value would lie within the calculated confidence interval in 95% of those samples.

# most of the times the extra step in the next lines is not necessary and this 
# line of code is enough
exp(cbind(
  OR = coef(logit), 
  confint(logit)))

eduyrs       1.0478581 1.0396365  1.0561731


Once we exponentiate the coefficient and obtain the odds ratio (OR), interpretation becomes more straightforward. The odds ratio tells us how the odds of the outcome change with a one-unit increase in a predictor variable. For example, if the odds ratio for political interest is below 1, this means that a one-unit increase in political interest decreases the odds of voting (compared to not voting). The same logic applies to the other variables in the model.
One final point about odds ratios—arguably the most intuitive way to interpret them—is to translate them into percentages.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Logistic function
The logistic function is : \[\begin{equation}
p_L (x) = \frac{1}{1+ e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(x-\mu)/s}} = \frac{e^{(x-\mu)/s}}{1+e^{(x-\mu)/s}}
\end{equation}\] and it is strictly bounded between 0 and 1, which is expected for a probability.

x <- c(1:10000)
mu <- 5000
s <- 500
plot(x, exp((x-mu)/s)/(1+exp((x-mu)/s)))








You can use this logistic function in the likelihood function: \[\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}(x) = \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 1)}^n p(x)_i \Pi_{i\  (y_i = 0)}^n (1 - p(x)_i),
\end{equation}\] maximize it, and find the parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that best fit your data.
This is the logic behind maximum likelihood estimation: you assume your probability follows a certain distribution (in this case, the logistic distribution), and then estimate the parameters that maximize the likelihood of obtaining your data. This is precisely what the glm function in R does when it fits a logistic regression model — it computes the parameters that maximize the likelihood function using numerical methods.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
The logistic regression
In logistic regression, coefficients represent the change in the log-odds of the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor variable, while holding all other variables constant. The sign of the coefficient indicates the direction of the relationship:

A positive coefficient means that as the predictor increases, the odds of the outcome increase.
A negative coefficient means that as the predictor increases, the odds of the outcome decrease.

To make interpretation more intuitive, we often convert coefficients into odds ratios by exponentiating them (this simply reverses the logarithm). The odds ratio represents how the odds of the outcome change for a one-unit increase in the predictor variable compared to a reference value.

An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates a positive association.
An odds ratio less than 1 indicates a negative association.

It is also important to remember that logistic regression relies on certain assumptions, including linearity in the logit, independence of observations, and appropriate model specification. Violations of these assumptions can affect both model performance and interpretation. We will revisit diagnostic checks for logistic regression models in a later session.
I know this may sound dense. It is somewhat technical, but it becomes much clearer once we apply the concepts to our actual model. Interpreting exponentiated coefficients as odds ratios will also make the results much more intuitive.
Looking at our model summary, we can already see that most independent variables are statistically significant (p < .05). Typically, we focus our interpretation on statistically significant variables and do not interpret those that are not significant.
From the results, we observe that closeness to a party and age are negatively associated with voting behavior. This makes sense given how the variables are coded. According to the codebook, higher values represent respondents who are less interested, less close to a party, or older (depending on the coding). Therefore, higher values correspond to a lower likelihood of voting on election day.
Trust in politicians, however, is coded in the opposite direction. Higher values indicate lower trust. As a result, the positive coefficient suggests that lower trust in politicians increases the likelihood of not voting. Ideally, it would have been better to code all independent variables in the same direction for easier interpretation, but the results can still be interpreted correctly as long as we carefully consider the coding scheme.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Predicted probabilities
Overall, we could now present a table with the odds ratios and move on to writing the paper. However, visualizing results often tells a much clearer and more compelling story. In this section, I will show you how to compute predicted probabilities and how to display them in an effective and visually appealing way.
In logistic regression, predicted probabilities represent the likelihood that an event occurs given specific values of the predictor variables. Rather than interpreting log-odds or odds ratios—which can feel abstract—predicted probabilities provide a simple number between 0 and 1. For instance, instead of stating that higher political interest increases the log-odds of voting, we can say that an individual with high political interest has a 75% probability of voting. This makes the results far more intuitive and easier to communicate.
Predicted probabilities are expressed on the original scale of the independent variables (IVs). This means they directly illustrate how changes in variables—such as political interest, trust in politicians, or education—affect the probability of the outcome. If political interest is measured on a scale from 1 to 4, we can examine how the probability of voting changes at each level of that scale, rather than simply noting whether the relationship is positive or negative. This is a major advantage over coefficient plots, which show direction and magnitude but not the actual likelihood of the outcome. Predicted probabilities therefore allow us to present findings in a way that is both intuitive and closely tied to the real-world measurement of our variables.
The key idea is that we select one predictor variable and decide the values at which we want to estimate the outcome. While doing so, we “hold the other independent variables constant.” This allows us to isolate the effect of the variable we are interested in.
To make this absolutely clear: when calculating predicted probabilities, we focus on one independent variable of interest and keep all other variables fixed—typically at their mean or median, or, in the case of a dummy variable, at one of its two possible values. By holding the other variables constant, we can clearly observe the independent effect of the predictor we care about.

# this package contains everything we need craft predicted probabilities and
# visualize them as well
library(ggeffects)

# like the predcit() function of Base R, we use ggpredict() and specify
# our variable of interest
predicted_probs <- ggpredict(logit, terms = "polintr")
predicted_probs

# Predicted probabilities of vote

polintr | Predicted |     95% CI
--------------------------------
      1 |      0.92 | 0.91, 0.92
      2 |      0.86 | 0.85, 0.87
      3 |      0.78 | 0.77, 0.78
      4 |      0.66 | 0.65, 0.67

Adjusted for:
* trstplt =    4.00
* trstprt =    4.00
* clsprty =    0.57
*    gndr =    0.54
*   yrbrn = 1969.00
*  eduyrs =   12.00

# this is the simplest way of plotting this
ggplot(predicted_probs, aes(x = x, y = predicted)) +
  # our graph is more or less a line, so geom_line() applies
  geom_line(color = "blue", size = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  # geom_ribbon() with the values that ggpredict() provided for the confidence
  # intervals then gives
  # us a shade around the geom_()line as CIs
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "grey", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of Voting by Political Interest",
    x = "Political Interest",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Voting"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10)
  )

  mutate(
    gender = x |> as.factor()
  ) |> 
  na.omit()

ggplot(predicted_probs_gender,
       aes(x = gender, y = predicted, fill = gender)) +

  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 5) +

       fill = "Gender") +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Automating processes
In programming, it often takes time to fully understand and apply new concepts. Once we become comfortable with a process, the next logical step is to think about how to automate it. Automation helps make our work faster, cleaner, and more efficient. After we understand a workflow well, we can usually transfer and automate it in other contexts with relatively little effort.
Take today’s logistic regression as an example. We worked with the ESS data and analyzed the 10th round for France, examining which variables predict abstention. But we could just as easily ask the same research question across multiple waves of the ESS or across multiple countries. If I asked you to run the same logit model for all ESS countries, your first instinct might be to copy and paste your code for each country. However, this would quickly lead to a very long and inelegant script—and the longer the code, the greater the risk of making mistakes.
A good rule of thumb in programming is this: if you find yourself repeating the same steps multiple times, and only a few elements (such as variable names or country identifiers) change, then the task can likely be automated. At some point, the goal should be to build a workflow—or pipeline—that allows your code to run as automatically and efficiently as possible.
In RStudio, there are several ways to achieve this. For example, you can use for-loops to perform the same operation sequentially over a list of elements. Alternatively, you can write your own functions. After all, functions such as glimpse() or read_csv2() were written by someone at some point. As R users, we can do the same. By creating our own functions, we can bundle multiple operations together and then apply them to several objects or subsets of a dataset—such as different countries—at once.
Everything that follows is optional, but I think it is important that you are exposed to these ideas early on. Some of you may already feel confident enough to experiment with automation on your own. If not, that is completely fine—you will get there. My goal here is simply to show you what is possible and to give you a sense of what you can achieve with R.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Functions in R
Functions in R are incredibly powerful and essential for efficient and automated programming. A function in R is defined using the function keyword. The basic structure includes the name of the function, a set of parameters, and the body where the actual computations are performed.
The basic syntax is as follows:
There are some minor conventions in RStudio when writing functions. Some of them also apply to other parts than just functions.

You should give them some “breathing” space. When you write the accolades, put a space bar in between.


#Bad
function(x){
  x + 1
}
#Good
function(x) {
  x + 1
}


You should always put a space between the equal sign and the value you assign to a variable. Place spaces around all infix operators (=, +, -, <-, etc.)


# this is bad
data<-read.csv("data.csv")
# this is good
data <- read.csv("data.csv")


“stretch” your code when possible ctrl + shift + a can be of help for that


# this is bad but in a longer example
country_model <- function(df) {glm(vote ~ polintr + trstplt + trstprt + clsprty + gndr + yrbrn + eduyrs, family = "binomial", data = df)
}
# this is better
country_model <- function(df) {
  glm(
    vote ~ polintr + trstplt + trstprt + clsprty + gndr + yrbrn + eduyrs,
    family = binomial(link = "logit"),
    data = df
  )
}


We usually assign verbs to functions. This means that the name of the function should be a verb that describes what the function does. If we want to create a function that reads the ESS files and does several operations at once, we should call it something like read_ess().

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
The purrr package
The purrr package in R is a powerful tool for handling repetitive tasks in a more efficient and elegant way. It is part of the Tidyverse, a collection of R packages designed to make data science faster, more intuitive, and more enjoyable.
In simple terms, purrr improves how we work with lists and vectors in R. It provides functions that allow us to apply operations—whether built-in functions or ones we write ourselves—to each element of a list or vector without explicitly writing loops. This approach is known as functional programming.
Put differently, the functions in purrr enable us to systematically apply a function to every element of a list or vector. Depending on which purrr function we use, the resulting output may differ (for example, returning a list, a vector, or a data frame). We can also control the structure of the output within the custom function that we pass to purrr, giving us both flexibility and efficiency.

The map function
The map() function from the purrr package in R is based on a straightforward but powerful idea: it applies a function to each element of a list or vector and returns a new list containing the results. This process is called mapping, which is why the function is named map().



The map function


Here’s how map() works in practice:

library(purrr)

# Example list of numbers
numbers <- list(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

# Apply the sqrt() function to each element using map()
sqrt_results <- map(numbers, sqrt)

# Print the results
print(sqrt_results)

[[1]]
[1] 1

[[2]]
[1] 1.414214

[[3]]
[1] 1.732051

[[4]]
[1] 2

[[5]]
[1] 2.236068

sqrt_results[1]

[[1]]
[1] 1

sqrt_results[[1]]

[1] 1

sqrt_results[[5]]

[1] 2.236068



Input: The main input to map() is a list or vector: in this example, the list with numbers (1,2,3,4,5). This can be as simple as a list of numbers or characters, or more complex objects like vectors within lists or even data frames.
Function Application: You provide a function that you want to apply to each element of the input. Here, the function is sqrt (square-root). This function can be a built-in R function or one you’ve written yourself. The important point is that it will be applied separately to each element of the list or vector.
Iteration: map() automatically iterates over each element of your input. There’s no need to write a loop—the function takes care of this internally. For each element, map() applies the function you specified.
Output: The results of the function applied to each element are collected into a new list. Each element of the output list corresponds to the result of the function applied to the respective element of the input.
Flexibility in Output Type: purrr offers specialized versions of map() to control the type of output. For instance, map_dbl() returns numeric values (doubles), map_chr() returns character vectors, and so on. This ensures that the output matches the type you expect, making subsequent analysis easier.

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Automating logistic regressions
Here, I present a code workflow that runs the logistic regression we’ve been working on, but simultaneously for all countries in the ESS. It also plots the odds ratio for our variable of interest, political interest, and compares McFadden’s pseudo R² (we’ll revisit this term in the next session).
To do this, I combine ideas from the optional section of Session 1 with the purrr package. The approach is to build one model per ESS country, then nest() the results into a new tibble. (Reminder: a tibble is a modern version of a data frame with enhanced printing and subsetting features.) Each row of this tibble contains all the information necessary for a single country-specific model. We then use map()`` to apply thetidy()` function from the broom package to each of these models.
Below is a simple function that takes a dataframe as input and returns a logistic regression model. Inside the function, I only specify the glm() call we’ve used before. The argument inside function()—in this example, df—is arbitrary; it can be any name you like. This name must appear somewhere inside the function, usually where the operation is applied to the input object. In our case, that’s in data = df.

country_model <- function(df) {
  glm(vote ~ polintr + trstplt + trstprt + clsprty + gndr + yrbrn + eduyrs, 
      family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = df)
}

To start, I import the ESS data and select only the variables that we want to use. I also perform some initial cleaning—removing unwanted observations or values—to make sure the dataset is ready for analysis.

# Recoding the 'vote' variable to binary (1 or 0)
# and filtering the dataset based on specified criteria
prepared_ess <- ess |> 
  mutate(vote = ifelse(vote == 1, 1, 0)) |> 
  filter(
    vote %in% c(0:1),
    polintr %in% c(1:4),
    clsprty %in% c(1:2),
    trstplt %in% c(0:10),
    trstprt %in% c(0:10),
    gndr %in% c(1:2),
    yrbrn %in% c(1900:2010),
    eduyrs %in% c(0:50)
  )

Then we will nest() the data as described (here)[https://luissattelmayer.github.io/quant-2025/session1/session1.html#nesting].

# library for McFadden pseudo R2
library(pscl)

Load the following packages :


library(ggeffects)

title: First homework - Logistic regressions
text:
Case study : gender and voting for the radical right
Recent debates in academia have focused on the impact of gender on voting for the radical right. While some scholars argue that women vote less for the radical right, others argue that this effect of gender may depend on the context. Some authors even suggest that the radical right has renewed its electoral appeal to women by developing so-called “femo-nationalism”—a form of nationalism that incorporates elements of feminism. This academic debate has also resonated in the public sphere, as illustrated by the Financial Times’ 2024 paper (Burn-Murdoch, 2024) entitled “A New Global Gender Divide Is Emerging”.



The radical right gender gap - Financial Times (2024)


For this reason, researchers have recently sought to understand whether gender has a positive or negative effect on voting for the radical right in France, particularly in the European and legislative elections (Piolat, N., Mayer, N., Durovic, A., 2025). Their papers are available here and here. In order to replicate and complement their findings, you are provided with a simplified dataset they used to conduct their analysis. Using R, you are asked to answer the following questions (by groups of 2 or 3) and submit the code you used in either a PDF or HTML file.

Download the dataset following https://github.com/scpo-quantimethods/quantitative_methods_two/raw/main/sessions/session2/data/poll2024.RData and import it into your local R environment.
If you are interested in how voting for the radical right varies by gender, determine:


Your dependent variable
Your independent variable Are they continuous, categorical ? Drop all the variables except second_round_vote, gender, union_member, diploma, religious_affiliation, income and birth_year.


The dataset is in .stata format. You can inspect the different values a variable takes by calling: attributes(data_set$variable) - it basically contains the codebook. Do that for variable second_round_vote. Then, create the following variables:


voteRN = 1 if the respondent voted for RN in the second round, 0 otherwise (NA if no answer)
Using 2026 as the reference year, create a variable age.


Define a variable female = 1 if the respondent identifies as a woman, 0 if male, and NA_integer_ otherwise (too few respondents in other categories or no answer).


Clean union_member, diploma, religion, and income by recoding non-responses as NA.
Create a nominal variable cohort by grouping ages into decades: 20-29, 30–39, 40–49, …, 80+, then run


data$cohort <- factor(
  data$cohort,
  levels = c("20-29","30-39","40-49","50-59","60-69","70-79","80+"),
  ordered = FALSE
)

to make sure the cohorts are logically ordered.

Plot a histogram of the age variable with 10 breaks. Identify the most frequent decade in the dataset.
Run a logistic regression predicting the probability of voting for RN based on gender and age. Interpret the results:


How does a one-year increase in age affect the odds of voting for RN?
How does being a woman affect the odds ratio?


Include as.factor(diploma) in the regression. Compare models using stargazer() by adapting the code below, which exponentiates the coefficients from your logistic regressions and adds the exponentiated values to the stargazer table:


exp_coef1 <- exp(coef(model1))
exp_coef2 <- exp(coef(model2))

exp_ci1 <- exp(confint(model1))
exp_ci2 <- exp(confint(model2))

stargazer(model1, model2,
          type = "text",            
          coef = list(exp_coef1, exp_coef2),
          ci = TRUE,
          ci.custom = list(exp_ci1, exp_ci2),
          p.auto = FALSE,
          title = "Logistic Regression (Odds Ratios)")

Interpret the results: How does attending a “grande école” affect the odds of voting for the RN? Is the coefficient on gender still significant ?

Include in the regression religion, union_member, and income. Only use as.factor(variable) for nominal variables with more than two categories. If it appears, disregard the following warning : Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred.


Compare your results. Some religious practices may substantially reduce the odds of voting for RN. Which religions are these? Are the results in line with your expectations?
Replace age with your cohort variable. Which cohort is most likely to vote for RN?


Run a logistic regression including the interaction age*female. Plot the interaction results using library(ggeffects) and ggpredict. Hint: use geom_ribbon() to display confidence intervals.
Run a similar regression with female*cohort and plot the interactions using library(ggeffects) and ggpredict(). Hint: use geom_errorbar() to display confidence intervals.
Bonus point: Repeat the analysis of question 8 and 9, 10 for the first round of legislative elections. Compare the results with the second round in a text of 5 lines max.

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)

# Simulate continuous independent variable
n <- 300
x <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Create probability using logistic function
true_prob <- 1 / (1 + exp(-( -1 + 2*x )))

# Generate binary outcome
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = true_prob)

data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Fit models
linear_model  <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
logit_model   <- glm(y ~ x, data = data, family = binomial)

# Create prediction grid
x_seq <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 200)
pred_data <- data.frame(x = x_seq)

pred_data$linear_pred <- predict(linear_model, newdata = pred_data)
pred_data$logit_pred  <- predict(logit_model, newdata = pred_data, type = "response")

# Plot
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Linear vs Logistic Regression for Binary Outcome",

library(ggplot2)

# Logistic function
logistic <- function(x, b0, b1) {
  1 / (1 + exp(-(b0 + b1 * x)))
}

# Create x grid
x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 400)

# Define parameter combinations
params <- data.frame(
  b0 = c(0, 0, -2, 2),
  b1 = c(1, 2, 1, 1),
  label = c("β0=0, β1=1 (baseline)",
            "β0=0, β1=2 (steeper)",
            "β0=-2, β1=1 (shift right)",
            "β0=2, β1=1 (shift left)")
)

# Generate predictions
plot_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:nrow(params), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    x = x,
    prob = logistic(x, params$b0[i], params$b1[i]),
    label = params$label[i]
  )
}))

# Plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = x, y = prob, color = label)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Effect of β0 and β1 in Logistic Regression",
       x = "X",

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Finding these parameters

Done through so-called maximum likelihood estimation, based on your data !
\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) is for one predictor
You can have k predictors : \[\begin{equation}
\mathcal{P}(Y = 1) = f_\mathcal{L}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 * X_1+\beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_3 +...+ \beta_k X_k))}}
\end{equation}\]
that can be continuous or categorical !

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text: Interpretation of logistic regression

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Odds ratio

You want to compare the probabilities of happening with probabilities of not happening…

\[\begin{equation}
\text{OR} = \frac{P(Y = 1)}{P(Y=0)} = \frac{P(Y = 1)}{1- P(Y=1)}
\end{equation}\]

If p = 0.1 : OR = 1/9
If p = 0.8 : OR = 8/2 = 4
if p = 0.5 : OR = 1
“how many times more or less likely to happen”

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Logit
\[\begin{equation}
\text{logit(p)} = \ln(\text{OR}) = \ln(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{P(Y=0)}) = \ln(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{1- P(Y=1)})
\end{equation}\]

If p = 0.1 : logit = ln(1/9) < 0
If p = 0.5 : logit = 0
If p = 0.8 : logit = ln(8/2) = 4 > 0
“how many times more or less likely to happen”

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)

# Simulate continuous independent variable
n <- 300
x <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Create probability using logistic function
true_prob <- 1 / (1 + exp(-( -1 + 2*x )))

# Generate binary outcome
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = true_prob)

data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# ---- Create 3 equal-width intervals of x ----
breaks <- seq(min(data$x), max(data$x), length.out = 4)
data$x_group <- cut(data$x, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)

# Fit models
linear_model  <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
logit_model   <- glm(y ~ x, data = data, family = binomial)

# Create prediction grid
x_seq <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 200)
pred_data <- data.frame(x = x_seq)

pred_data$linear_pred <- predict(linear_model, newdata = pred_data)
pred_data$logit_pred  <- predict(logit_model, newdata = pred_data, type = "response")

# Plot

  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.6) +

An example : ESS with French data

Use mutate and case_when to transform these data :


data %>% mutate(new_value = case_when(
    condition1 ~ value_if_true1,
    condition2 ~ value_if_true2,
    TRUE ~ default_value
  ))


ess <- ess |> 
  mutate(
    vote = case_when(
      vote %in% c(3, 7, 8, 9) ~ NA_integer_,
      TRUE ~ vote
  ))
table(ess$vote)


   1    2 
1025  590 



You can group the operations :


ess_final <- ess |> 
  # mutating the dependent variable to get rid of any unnecessary rows
  # as we have done above
  mutate(
    vote = case_when(
      vote %in% c(3, 7, 8, 9) ~ NA_integer_,
      vote == 2 ~ 0,
      vote == 1 ~ 1, 
      TRUE ~ vote
    ),
    # Recode 'polintr' to drop values 7 to 9
    polintr = case_when(
      polintr %in% c(7:9) ~ NA_integer_,
      TRUE ~ polintr
    ),
    # Recode 'clsprty' 1/2 into 0/1 and drop 7, 8
    clsprty = case_when(
      clsprty == 1 ~ 0,
      clsprty == 2 ~ 1,
      clsprty %in% c(7, 8) ~ NA_integer_,
      TRUE ~ clsprty
    ),
    # Recode 'gndr' into 0/1 and handle other cases as NAs
    gndr = case_when(
      gndr == 1 ~ 0,
      gndr == 2 ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    # recode eduyrs
    eduyrs = case_when(
      eduyrs %in% c(1:55) ~ eduyrs,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ),
    # this one is very advanced...
    across(c(trstplt, trstprt), ~case_when(
      .x <= 10 ~ .x, 
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_
    ))
  )

library(ggplot2)

logistic <- function(x, b0, b1) {

params <- data.frame(

  )
}))

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Finding these parameters

Done through so-called maximum likelihood estimation, based on your data !
\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) is for one predictor
You can have k predictors : \[\begin{equation}
\mathcal{P}(Y = 1) = f_\mathcal{L}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 * X_1+\beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_3 +...+ \beta_k X_k))}}
\end{equation}\]
that can be continuous or categorical !

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Odds ratio

You want to compare the probabilities of happening with probabilities of not happening…

\[\begin{equation}
\text{OR} = \frac{P(Y = 1)}{P(Y=0)} = \frac{P(Y = 1)}{1- P(Y=1)}
\end{equation}\]

If p = 0.1 : OR = 1/9
If p = 0.8 : OR = 8/2 = 4
if p = 0.5 : OR = 1
“how many times more or less likely to happen”

title: Session 2 : logistic regressions
text:
Logit
\[\begin{equation}
\text{logit(p)} = \ln(\text{OR}) = \ln(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{P(Y=0)}) = \ln(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{1- P(Y=1)})
\end{equation}\]

If p = 0.1 : logit = ln(1/9) < 0
If p = 0.5 : logit = 0
If p = 0.8 : logit = ln(8/2) = 4 > 0
“how many times more or less likely to happen”
